# The Working Accord: full text

## The Working Accord: Ten Rules for Sharing Work With AI
URL: https://workingaccord.ca/

Machines take the repetition. People keep the judgment. Ten rules for sharing work with AI. A public commitment any employer can sign, and any worker can hold them to. Lewis Hine, Power house mechanic working on steam pump , 1920 Every machine that took a job came with the same promise: the work comes back. It did. Not for the weaver. Not for the switchboard operator. Not for the bookkeeping clerk. Some jobs will go to AI too. This time, we write down what those people are owed before it happens. See who paid last time Cutting jobs is not a reason to use AI. If the business case is a smaller payroll, it isn't a plan. Decide what the work should look like first. Then decide who does it, and what the people it changes are owed: notice, retraining, and a share of what the software saves. Read rule 10 31% of Canadian employees work in jobs highly exposed to AI where some tasks could be replaced by it. Another 29% are in exposed jobs where AI is more likely to support the work. Statistics Canada, 2024, using 2021 census data. The ten rules Written for the person on the line and the person signing the purchase order. Employers sign all ten, or none. 01 Machines take the repetition. People keep the judgment. Repetitive work is real work, and for some people it is the whole job. When a machine takes it on, the person doing it is owed rules 8 and 9. 02 A person signs off on anything that matters. Safety, money, health and people's jobs. The person signing can overrule the machine, gets time to check its work, and is never penalized for saying no. 03 Questioning the tool is part of the job. A tool can be wrong, unsafe, a privacy risk, or a bad fit for the work. Saying so, with reasons, is doing the job well. 04 Show the work, the machine's and yours. Say what the software did and what you did. Nobody passes off a machine's draft as their own thinking, starting with the people in charge. 05 Keep the skill to check it. AI is strong at some tasks and confidently wrong at others. New hires learn the job itself, not just how to prompt for it. 06 No secret scorekeeping. No one is disciplined or laid off because software ranked them. Where it watches or ranks people at all, they're told first and shown what it said. 07 Your know-how is not free training data. When an experienced worker's knowledge trains the system, they're told, credited and paid for it. 08 Time saved gets shared, in writing. At least half of freed hours go back to the people doing the work: higher pay, paid training, or better work. Reported every quarter. 09 If a job is going to change or go, the person hears first. At least 90 days' notice, or the legal minimum if longer. First claim on any new role. Paid retraining. Severance on top, not instead. 10 A headcount number is not a plan. A layoff lands on people and families, not on a spreadsheet. Decide what the work should look like before deciding who does it. What the rules look like on the job Some of these are measured in studies. Some are illustrations we wrote to show the rules at work, and they're labelled. See 68 jobs, before and after Illustration Line inspector, food plant Used to pull defects off the line by eye for a whole shift. Now a camera flags them, and the inspector decides what actually gets pulled. When the camera misses something, she teaches it, and that teaching is part of her paid job. Rules 2 and 7 Illustration Maintenance tech Used to find out a bearing failed when the line stopped. Now gets a flag that vibration is trending up, and decides whether to pull the line at lunch or wait for Friday. The tech can ignore the flag if it's wrong. Rules 2 and 3 Illustration. A job that goes away. Order-entry clerk Keys about 300 orders a day from emails and PDFs. The system starts reading the orders, and the data-entry role goes away. Under the accord, the clerk is told 90 days before rollout, gets paid retraining on the orders the system gets wrong with first claim on that role, and severance either way. Rule 9 Study Support desk, one software company 5,172 agents got an AI assistant and resolved 15% more issues per hour on average. The lowest-skilled fifth gained the most, about 36%. The most experienced barely sped up, and their quality dipped slightly. The assistant learned from the best agents' own conversations. Nothing in the study says they were paid more for it. Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, 2025. One Fortune 500 firm. Rule 7 Study Breast screening in Sweden AI sorted mammograms and flagged areas, and radiologists made every call. An early analysis found similar detection with 44% less screen reading. With about 106,000 women, the AI-supported group found 29% more cancers, and a 2026 follow-up found missed cancers no more common. Less reading means fewer radiologist hours per screen. A health system can screen more women, or employ fewer radiologists. Lång 2023, Hernström 2025, Gommers 2026. Rule 8 Study. Where it didn't help. Experienced programmers 16 experienced open-source developers took 19% longer on real tasks when allowed AI tools, while believing they'd been about 20% faster. METR, 2025, which now calls the result dated for newer tools. Rule 5 The work comes back. Not always for the same people. New tools create more work than they destroy. History is clear on that. It's just as clear that the new work rarely goes to the people who lost the old work. 20s to 6s Handloom weavers, 1806 to 1830 Weekly pay fell from about 20 shillings to about 6, and real wages to about a quarter of the peak. Wages across Britain took about two generations to catch up with output. 7 pts Telephone operators, 1920s to 1940 Operators over 25 were about 7 points less likely to be working ten years after dial phones arrived, and those working were more likely in lower-paying jobs. 50 to 70% Routine-task workers, 1980 to 2016 Automation explains 50% to 70% of the change in the US wage structure, mostly through falling relative pay for people whose tasks were automated. 19% Young workers, now In the most AI-exposed US jobs, employment of 22 to 25 year olds has fallen 19% behind less-exposed jobs in the latest data, up from 13% in the first release, mostly through less hiring. 0 Pay, so far A large Danish study found AI chatbots had no measurable effect yet on average earnings or hours. The gains aren't reaching paycheques on their own. Who should be worried Not the people doing the work. These people. Anyone whose AI plan is a headcount number. Cut first and you find out later what the people you let go actually knew: which supplier fudges specs, which machine runs hot in July, which customer is about to leave. Managers who let software do the ranking. A score you can't explain is not a reason to discipline anyone. Rule 6 ends that. Employers who won't pay for training. In a study of 5,172 support agents, the least-skilled gained the most. Those are the people a training budget is for. Cut it, and the people the tools could help most are left to figure it out alone. Leaders who stopped learning. When work changes, the people making the decisions have to learn fastest. A boss who can't say what the software does can't tell when it's wrong, or explain a decision to the person it lands on. Anyone hiding what the software does. If you can't tell people what it's for, you already know what they'd say. Rules 4 and 6 . People have worried about this before, often with good reason Several of these worries came true for the people who had them, even when things worked out for everyone else. Read the full history . ← → 370 BC Writing will weaken memory. We kept writing. He had a point: most of us no longer memorize long texts. Plato 1492 Printing will end copying by hand. Hand-copying did fade. Books reached millions who had never owned one. Trithemius 1811 Machines will wreck weavers' pay. It came true for them. The Luddites fought over wages and who got the gains, and were put down by force. Hobsbawm 1920 Dial phones will end operators' jobs. They mostly did. Older operators were hit hardest. Younger women moved into other work. Feigenbaum and Gross 1930 "Technological unemployment." Keynes called it "a temporary phase of maladjustment." Temporary can still mean years for a family. Keynes 1966 Automation will cause mass unemployment. A US commission found "technology eliminates jobs, not work," and recommended public jobs, a guaranteed income and education for displaced workers. Bowen commission 1988 ATMs will end bank tellers. Not at first: fewer tellers per branch, but many more branches. Now the US projects about 13% fewer tellers over the next decade. Bessen; BLS 1980s Spreadsheets will end accounting work. 400,000 clerk jobs went; 600,000 accounting jobs arrived. The clerks were mostly women. The source doesn't say where they went. NPR; Women's Bureau 2018 All of the above. About 60% of US jobs had titles that didn't exist in 1940. The middle has thinned. Autor et al. If your workplace is changing, ask these Ask for the answers in writing. If you have a union, bring these to your rep. The full worker guide . Which tasks will the software take on, and whose jobs are they? Who signs off on what it does, and can they overrule it? Will it monitor, rate or rank me? Will I see what it says? If it saves hours, where do they go, and who decides? If my role changes or goes: how much notice, what training, what severance? Sign the accord Workers sign to say these rules are the floor. ## The Ten Rules for How People and AI Share Work
URL: https://workingaccord.ca/accord/

Home / The ten rules The ten rules The Working Accord is ten rules for bringing AI into a workplace fairly. A person signs off on anything that matters. Nobody is secretly scored by software. Time the software saves is shared in writing. Anyone whose job will change or go hears first, with notice, retraining and severance. Employers sign all ten or none. Version 1.0, October 2026. Free to use, copy and adapt. Jump to a rule 1. Repetition and judgment 2. A person signs off 3. Questioning the tool 4. Show the work 5. Keep the skill 6. No secret scorekeeping 7. Know-how isn't free 8. Share the time saved 9. Hear it first 10. Headcount isn't a plan 01 Machines take the repetition. People keep the judgment. Software takes on repetitive tasks; decisions that need judgment stay with people. What it asks List which tasks the software will do and which decisions stay with people, before it goes in. Why Repetitive work is real work, and for some people it's the whole job. Naming the tasks up front is how you find out whose job changes, which is what rules 8 and 9 are for. 02 A person signs off on anything that matters. Decisions about safety, money, health or people's jobs need a named person's approval, not just a model's output. What it asks The person signing can overrule the software, gets enough time to actually check its work, and is never penalized for saying no. Why A sign-off without time or authority is a rubber stamp. In one study, consultants who leaned on AI for a task it was weak at got the right answer 19 points less often than those who didn't. 03 Questioning the tool is part of the job. Raising a concern about an AI tool, with reasons, counts as doing the job well. What it asks A clear way to flag that a tool is wrong, unsafe, a privacy risk or a bad fit, and a response within a set time. Why The people closest to the work see the failures first. If questioning the tool looks like resisting change, they stop saying anything. 04 Show the work, the machine's and yours. Say what the software produced and what you added, at every level of the organization. What it asks Nobody passes off a machine's draft as their own thinking, starting with the people in charge. Why Credit and blame should land on the right place. It also tells the next person how much to trust the result. 05 Keep the skill to check it. People must stay able to do and judge the work themselves, so someone can tell when the software is wrong. What it asks New hires learn the job itself, not just how to prompt for it. Teams practise the task without the tool often enough to keep the skill. Why Feeling faster isn't being faster. In a 2025 trial, experienced programmers took 19% longer with AI tools while believing they'd been about 20% faster. 06 No secret scorekeeping. No one is disciplined or laid off because software ranked them, and nobody is watched or ranked by software without being told. What it asks A software ranking is never the reason for discipline or a layoff; the person deciding must be able to explain the decision without it. Where software watches or ranks people at all, they're told first and shown what it says about them, with a way to correct it. Why People can't fix a record they can't see. Canada's federal Privacy Commissioner says workplace monitoring should be "specific, targeted and appropriate in the circumstances." This rule adds that people are told. 07 Your know-how is not free training data. When an experienced worker's knowledge is used to train a system, they're told, credited and paid for it. What it asks Tell people before their work is used to train a system, name them where it's used, and pay for it as the valuable work it is. Why In a field study of 5,172 support agents, an assistant learned from the best support agents' conversations and lifted everyone else. Nothing in the study says the best agents were paid more for it. 08 Time saved gets shared, in writing. Before software goes in, the team and management agree in writing how freed-up hours will be used, and at least half go back to the people doing the work. What it asks At least half of the saved time goes to higher pay, paid training or better work. Fewer overtime hours only count if take-home pay holds. The split is reported to the team every quarter. Why Gains don't reach paycheques on their own. A large Danish study found AI chatbots had no measurable effect yet on average earnings or hours. 09 If a job is going to change or go, the person hears first. Anyone whose role will change or end because of software gets notice, retraining and severance before it happens. What it asks At least 90 days' notice, or the legal minimum if that is longer. First claim on any new role the change creates. Paid retraining. Severance above the legal minimum, on top of retraining, not instead of it. Why When telephone exchanges switched to dial, operators over 25 were about 7 points less likely to be working ten years later. The cost of a transition lands hardest on the people already in the job. 10 A headcount number is not a plan. Decide what the work should look like before deciding who does it. What it asks No AI project is approved on a headcount target alone. The plan names the work, the people affected, and how rules 8 and 9 will be met. Why A layoff lands on people and families, not on a spreadsheet. And a plan built only on a smaller payroll usually skips the work of finding out what the software is actually good at. Signing the accord. Workers sign to say these rules are the floor. Employers sign all ten as a commitment and are listed with the date. Sign the accord or read the employer guide . The evidence Who paid last time For workers Questions to ask your employer For employers How to adopt the rules

## AI and Job Losses: What the Evidence Says, and Who Paid
URL: https://workingaccord.ca/evidence/

Home / Evidence The work comes back. Not always for the same people. History shows new technology creates more work than it destroys, but often not for the people who lose the old work, and not quickly. Handloom weavers' pay fell to about a quarter of its peak. Older telephone operators were less likely to be working a decade after dial phones. Today, young workers in AI-exposed jobs are being hired less. Last reviewed October 2026. Every figure links to its source. Photo: telephone operators, 1927, US National Archives. Questions on this page How many Canadian jobs are exposed? Is AI causing job losses? Does technology create more jobs? What happened to the weavers? What happened to telephone operators? What does automation do to pay? Which jobs will AI replace? Does AI help the people who use it? How many Canadian jobs are exposed to AI? Among Canadian employees aged 18 to 64, about 31% work in jobs highly exposed to AI with low "complementarity", meaning some of their tasks could be replaced by AI in future. Another 29% are in highly exposed jobs where AI is more likely to support the work, and about 40% are in jobs that aren't highly exposed. Statistics Canada estimated this from 2021 census data and published it in 2024. "Highly exposed" means above the median for all occupations. Exposure is not the same as job loss. It measures how much of a job's tasks AI could do, not what employers will choose to do with it. Is AI causing job losses in Canada? There is no official Canadian count of jobs lost to AI yet. The clearest early signal comes from US payroll data: employment of 22 to 25 year olds in the most AI-exposed jobs fell 13% relative to less-exposed jobs in the first release, widening to 19% in the 2026 update, mostly through less hiring. Experienced workers showed no gap. The authors call this a warning sign, not proof that AI caused it. Some jobs will be lost to AI. The open question is who carries the cost. Does new technology create more jobs than it destroys? Over long periods, yes. About 60% of US jobs in 2018 had titles that didn't exist in 1940. In 1966 a US presidential commission concluded that "technology eliminates jobs, not work." But the same research shows where the new work went. Since 1980 it has been mostly well-paid professional jobs and low-paid service jobs, while middle-paying jobs thinned. The 1966 commission itself recommended public service jobs, a guaranteed minimum income and education for people displaced in the meantime. What happened to weavers during the Industrial Revolution? Handloom weavers' weekly pay fell from about 20 shillings in 1806 to about 6 by 1830, and their real wages fell to roughly a quarter of the peak. Across Britain, output per worker rose 46% between 1780 and 1840 while real wages rose 12%. Wages took until the second half of the century to catch up, about two generations. What happened to telephone operators when calls were automated? When US cities switched to dial phones between the 1920s and 1940, operator jobs for young women fell sharply. Operators over 25 were about 7 percentage points less likely to be working at all ten years later, and those still working were more likely to be in lower-paying jobs. Younger women overall found other work, in typing and secretarial jobs and in lower-wage service work. The cost landed hardest on the people already in the job. What does automation do to wages? Automation explains 50% to 70% of the change in the US wage structure between 1980 and 2016, mostly through falling relative pay for workers whose routine tasks were automated. For AI chatbots so far, a large Danish study found no measurable effect on average earnings or hours, up or down. The gains aren't reaching paycheques on their own. That's the case for rule 8 . Which jobs will AI replace by 2030? Nobody can name them with confidence, and be wary of anyone who does. Research measures which tasks AI could do, not which jobs employers will cut. Jobs made mostly of tasks AI can do on its own, with little need for human judgment, are the most exposed. What history does show: the people most at risk are those already in a job when it changes, especially later in their careers. That's who rule 9 is for. Does AI help the people who use it? Sometimes a lot, sometimes not at all, and sometimes it makes things worse. It depends on the task. Support desk: 5,172 agents at one Fortune 500 software company resolved 15% more issues per hour with an AI assistant. The lowest-skilled fifth gained about 36%. The most experienced barely sped up and their quality dipped slightly. Breast screening, Sweden: AI sorted mammograms and flagged areas, and radiologists made every call. An early analysis of 80,033 women found similar cancer detection with 44% less screen reading. With 105,934 women, the AI-supported group detected 29% more cancers. In 2026, cancers missed between screenings were no more common with AI (1.55 vs 1.76 per 1,000), which the authors class as no worse, not proven better. Consultants: on tasks AI was good at, consultants finished more work faster with higher quality. On a task it was weak at, AI users were 19 percentage points less likely to get it right. Experienced programmers: took 19% longer on real tasks when allowed AI tools, while believing they'd been about 20% faster. History People have worried about this before The answer The ten rules For workers What to ask your employer

## Luddites to ATMs: A History of Fears About Technology
URL: https://workingaccord.ca/history/

Home / History People have worried about this before, often with good reason Every major work technology, from the power loom to the ATM, came with fears that it would destroy jobs. Over decades, new work always appeared. But several of those fears came true for the people who had them: the Luddite weavers, the telephone operators, and the bookkeeping clerks all paid real costs while others gained. Last reviewed October 2026. Photo: women pairing fuze components, General Engineering Company (Canada), Scarborough, Ontario, about 1943. Archives of Ontario. On this page Who were the Luddites? Were the Luddites right? Telephone operators Did ATMs reduce bank tellers? Spreadsheets and bookkeepers Technological unemployment Older fears: writing and printing The pattern Who were the Luddites, and what did they actually want? The Luddites were English textile workers who broke machines between 1811 and 1816. They weren't against technology as such. The historian Eric Hobsbawm called machine-breaking "collective bargaining by riot": a way to pressure employers over wages and working conditions at a time when unions were illegal. Today "Luddite" is used to mean someone who fears new technology. The original Luddites were fighting over who got the gains from it. They were put down by force, including executions. Were the Luddites right? About their own lives, largely yes. Handloom weavers' weekly pay fell from about 20 shillings in 1806 to about 6 by 1830. Across Britain, wages lagged far behind output for roughly two generations before catching up in the second half of the 1800s. Their grandchildren were better off. They weren't. Bell Telephone exchange, Montreal, about 1898. Within a few decades, dial switching took most of these jobs. What happened to telephone operators? Between the 1920s and 1940, AT&T automated more than half of the US telephone network with dial switching. Most young women's operator jobs disappeared. Operators over 25 were about 7 percentage points less likely to be working at all ten years later, and those still working were more likely to be in lower-paying jobs. Later generations of young women found other work, much of it lower-wage. Did ATMs reduce the number of bank tellers? Not at first. Between 1988 and 2004, tellers per urban bank branch fell from 20 to 13, but banks opened 43% more urban branches, so teller jobs held. Then the decline came. US teller jobs fell from about 600,500 in 2008 to 339,200 in 2025, and the government projects about 13% fewer over the next decade. The ATM story is often told as proof that automation never costs jobs. It's better read as proof that the effect can arrive late. Did spreadsheets end accounting jobs? Bookkeeping jobs, partly. Since 1980, about 400,000 US bookkeeping and accounting clerk jobs went away, and about 600,000 accounting jobs were added. The clerks were mostly women: in 1980 it was one of the ten most common jobs for American women, and it is still about 86% women today. The show didn't say where they went, and we couldn't find anyone who tracked it. The new accounting jobs usually required a degree. What is technological unemployment? Technological unemployment is job loss caused by labour-saving technology arriving faster than new uses for labour. John Maynard Keynes described it in 1930 as "a temporary phase of maladjustment." He was right about the direction. But temporary can still mean years, or a career, for the people living through it. Did people fear writing and printing too? Yes. In Plato's Phaedrus , Socrates warns that writing will "produce forgetfulness" in those who learn it. In 1492 the abbot Johannes Trithemius argued hand-copying was better than printing, though he didn't oppose printing itself. Both had a point: we no longer memorize long texts, and hand-copying did fade. Both also missed what the new tool made possible. The pattern Three things repeat across 200 years: The work comes back. New kinds of jobs have always appeared, often ones nobody predicted. It doesn't come back for the same people. The cost falls on whoever is in the job when it changes, especially later in their careers. Who gets the gains is a choice. It was decided by laws, unions and employers, not by the machines. The Working Accord is about the third point. Read the ten rules . Evidence What's happening now The answer The ten rules Questions AI and jobs, answered

## AI at Work: Your Rights and Questions to Ask in Canada
URL: https://workingaccord.ca/workers/

Home / For workers If your workplace is changing If your employer is bringing in AI, ask five questions, in writing: which tasks it takes on, who signs off on it, whether it monitors you, where saved hours go, and what happens if your role changes. In Canada you also have legal rights to notice or pay if your job ends, and free help with retraining. Not legal advice. Last reviewed October 2026. On this page Five questions to ask What the law already gives you Where to get help If you have a union Five questions to ask your employer Ask for the answers in writing. You can also ask which of the ten rules your employer will commit to, and check whether it has signed the accord . Which tasks will the software take on, and whose jobs are they? Who signs off on what it does, and can they overrule it? Will it monitor, rate or rank me? Will I see what it says? If it saves hours, where do they go, and who decides? If my role changes or goes: how much notice, what training, what severance? What the law already gives you What notice am I owed if my job ends? It depends on your province, how long you've worked there, and how many people are let go. Each province sets minimum notice or pay in lieu for individual layoffs, and common law often requires more. When 50 or more people are let go within four weeks, longer group notice applies: in Manitoba , 10 weeks for 50 to 100 people, 14 weeks for 101 to 299, and 18 weeks for 300 or more; in Ontario , 8 weeks for 50 to 199, 12 weeks for 200 to 499, and 16 weeks for 500 or more. Federally regulated employers must give at least 16 weeks. This isn't legal advice. Can my employer monitor me with AI? Employers can monitor work in Canada, within limits. The federal Privacy Commissioner's guidance says workplace monitoring should be "specific, targeted and appropriate in the circumstances" ( Privacy in the Workplace ). Privacy rules differ by province and sector. The accord goes further: nobody is watched or ranked by software without being told first and shown what it says ( rule 6 ). Can my employer replace me with AI? In most of Canada, an employer can eliminate a role for business reasons, including automation, if it gives the notice or pay in lieu required by employment standards law. Many workers are owed more under common law "reasonable notice", and unionized workers may have technological change protections. Get advice for your own situation. Where to get help Find your province's employment standards A Government of Canada page that links each province and territory's rules on notice, severance and termination. Federal termination rules For banks, telecom, transport and other federally regulated employers. Employment Insurance regular benefits If your job ends. EI while you train How to keep EI while taking approved courses. Government of Canada training programs Skills and retraining programs. Job Bank: find training Training programs by province. Privacy in the workplace The federal Privacy Commissioner on workplace monitoring. If you have a union A collective agreement gives you a say. Many agreements include technological change clauses, and Canadian unions are now bargaining over AI directly; Unifor has negotiated AI terms in recent agreements. The Canadian Labour Congress is calling for labour law to be updated for AI. Bring the five questions above to your rep. The ten rules are written so they can be used in bargaining, word for word. Add your name Sign the accord The evidence Who paid last time Questions More answers

## How Canadian Employers Can Bring In AI Fairly
URL: https://workingaccord.ca/employers/

Home / For employers Bringing in AI without losing your people Tell people early, decide who signs off, share what the software saves, and give anyone whose job changes notice, retraining and severance. That's most of the accord. The rest of this page turns the ten rules into a checklist you can use before any AI project is approved. Last reviewed October 2026. On this page Before you buy During rollout After it's running Signing the accord The difference between a change that lifts people and one that frightens them is rarely the software. It comes down to whether people are told early, trained properly, and given a share of what the change saves. Before you buy Name the tasks. List which tasks the software will do and which decisions stay with people. Note whose jobs those tasks belong to. ( Rule 1 ) Don't approve on a headcount number. The plan names the work, the people affected, and how you'll meet rules 8 and 9. ( Rule 10 ) Tell people now. Before the decision is final, in writing, with a real way to raise concerns. ( Rule 3 ) Check monitoring. If the tool can watch, rate or rank people, decide now whether you'll use that, and plan to tell them. ( Rule 6 ) Employers sign all ten , or none. No picking the easy ones. Signers are listed with the date, and breach reports are noted on the list with whether the employer answered. Sign as an employer During rollout Name the person who signs off on anything touching safety, money, health or jobs, and give them the time and authority to say no. ( Rule 2 ) Agree the time split in writing. At least half of saved hours go to higher pay, paid training or better work. ( Rule 8 ) Pay for know-how. If experienced staff's work trains the system, tell them, credit them and pay them. ( Rule 7 ) Give notice early. At least 90 days, or the legal minimum if longer, before any role changes or ends, with retraining and first claim on new roles. ( Rule 9 ) After it's running Report the time split to the team every quarter. Keep the skill. Train new hires on the job itself, and practise without the tool often enough to catch its mistakes. ( Rule 5 ) Show the work. Make it normal to say what the software produced and what people added. ( Rule 4 ) What does the law already require? Employment standards set minimum notice or pay for terminations, with longer group notice when 50 or more people are let go within four weeks: 10 to 18 weeks in Manitoba , 8 to 16 weeks in Ontario , and at least 16 weeks for federally regulated employers . Since January 1, 2026, Ontario employers with 25 or more employees must say in public job postings if AI is used to screen, assess or select applicants ( Osler summary ). The Privacy Commissioner says monitoring should be "specific, targeted and appropriate" ( guidance ). Unionized workplaces may have technological change clauses. The accord sets a floor above all of these; get legal advice for your situation. Signing the accord Employers sign all ten rules, or don't sign. No picking the easy ones. Signers are listed with the date. If a worker reports a breach, we ask you to answer, and we note on the list that a question was raised and whether you answered. Sign as an employer

## AI and Jobs in Canada: Your Questions Answered
URL: https://workingaccord.ca/faq/

Home / Questions AI and jobs in Canada, answered Short, sourced answers to the questions Canadians ask most about AI and work. Each answer starts with the plain answer, then the evidence. Nothing here is legal advice; for your own situation, contact your provincial employment standards office or your union. Last reviewed October 2026. Jobs and the evidence Will AI take my job? What jobs will AI replace? What jobs are safe from AI? How many Canadian jobs are exposed to AI? Is AI causing job losses in Canada? Does new technology create more jobs than it destroys? Does AI make workers more productive? Your rights in Canada Can my employer replace me with AI? Can my employer use AI to monitor me at work in Canada? What notice am I owed if I'm laid off in Manitoba or Ontario? Where can I get retraining help in Canada after a layoff? Do unions have a say in how AI is introduced? For employers What should an AI policy for the workplace include? How should an employer tell staff about AI before bringing it in? History Who were the Luddites? Did ATMs reduce the number of bank tellers? What is technological unemployment? About the accord What is The Working Accord? Who is behind The Working Accord? Why would a company that makes AI software write this? Jobs and the evidence Will AI take my job? Probably not all of it, but it may change it a lot. Research measures which tasks AI can do, and most jobs are a mix of tasks. Jobs made mostly of tasks AI can do alone are the most exposed. The people most at risk historically are those already in a job when it changes, especially later in their careers. The better question is what you're owed if it does change. See the worker guide . What jobs will AI replace? No one can say with confidence. Lists of "jobs AI will replace" are guesses. What research shows is that AI is most likely to take over tasks that are routine, text- or data-based, and don't need much judgment. In US payroll data, the clearest early effect is fewer young people being hired into the most AI-exposed jobs. What jobs are safe from AI? No job is fully safe, and few will vanish outright. Work that depends on judgment, physical skill in changing settings, trust and care is the hardest to automate. In Canada, about 40% of employees are in jobs Statistics Canada does not rate as highly exposed to AI. How many Canadian jobs are exposed to AI? Among Canadian employees aged 18 to 64, about 31% work in jobs highly exposed to AI with low "complementarity", meaning some of their tasks could be replaced by AI in future. Another 29% are in highly exposed jobs where AI is more likely to support the work, and about 40% are in jobs that aren't highly exposed. Statistics Canada estimated this from 2021 census data and published it in 2024. "Highly exposed" means above the median for all occupations. Is AI causing job losses in Canada? There's no official Canadian count yet. The clearest early evidence is from the US, where employment of 22 to 25 year olds in the most AI-exposed jobs has fallen behind less-exposed jobs, by 19% in the latest data, mostly through less hiring. The researchers call it a warning sign, not proof of cause. More on the evidence . Does new technology create more jobs than it destroys? Over decades, yes: about 60% of US jobs in 2018 had titles that didn't exist in 1940. But the new jobs often go to different people, and the transition can take a generation. Read who paid last time . Does AI make workers more productive? Sometimes. At one large support desk, AI raised issues resolved per hour by 15%, and by about 36% for the least-skilled agents. But experienced programmers in a 2025 trial were 19% slower with AI while believing they were faster. It depends on the task, which is why people need to keep the skill to check it. Your rights in Canada Can my employer replace me with AI? In most of Canada, an employer can eliminate a role for business reasons, including automation, as long as it gives the notice or pay in lieu required by employment standards law. Many workers are also owed longer "reasonable notice" under common law, and unionized workers may have technological change protections in their collective agreement. This isn't legal advice: check with your provincial employment standards office, a lawyer, or your union. Can my employer use AI to monitor me at work in Canada? Employers can monitor work in Canada, within limits. The federal Privacy Commissioner's guidance says workplace monitoring should be "specific, targeted and appropriate in the circumstances" ( Privacy in the Workplace ). Privacy rules differ by province and sector. The accord goes further: nobody is watched or ranked by software without being told first and shown what it says ( rule 6 ). What notice am I owed if I'm laid off in Manitoba or Ontario? It depends on your province, how long you've worked there, and how many people are let go. Each province sets minimum notice or pay in lieu for individual layoffs, and common law often requires more. When 50 or more people are let go within four weeks, longer group notice applies: in Manitoba , 10 weeks for 50 to 100 people, 14 weeks for 101 to 299, and 18 weeks for 300 or more; in Ontario , 8 weeks for 50 to 199, 12 weeks for 200 to 499, and 16 weeks for 500 or more. Federally regulated employers must give at least 16 weeks. This isn't legal advice. Where can I get retraining help in Canada after a layoff? Start with Employment Insurance regular benefits if you've lost your job; in some cases you can keep receiving EI while you take approved training . The federal training page and Job Bank list programs by province, and your provincial employment office may fund retraining. Do unions have a say in how AI is introduced? Yes, where there's a collective agreement. Many agreements include technological change clauses, and Canadian unions are now bargaining over AI directly; Unifor has negotiated AI terms in recent agreements. The Canadian Labour Congress is calling for labour law to be updated for AI. The ten rules are written so they can be used in bargaining word for word. For employers What should an AI policy for the workplace include? At minimum: which tasks the software will do and which decisions stay with people; who signs off; whether it monitors anyone; how saved time is shared; and what happens to anyone whose job changes, including notice, retraining and severance. Those are the core of the ten rules of The Working Accord. Read the employer guide . How should an employer tell staff about AI before bringing it in? Early, in writing, and before the decision is final. Say which tasks the software will take on, whose jobs that touches, whether it monitors anyone, and how saved time will be used. Give people a real way to raise concerns. History Who were the Luddites? English textile workers who broke machines between 1811 and 1816. They weren't against technology itself; they were fighting over wages and who got the gains, at a time when unions were illegal. More history . Did ATMs reduce the number of bank tellers? Not at first. Fewer tellers worked in each branch, but banks opened many more branches, so teller jobs held for years. The US government now projects about 13% fewer tellers over the next decade. The full story . What is technological unemployment? Job loss caused by labour-saving technology arriving faster than new uses for labour. Keynes called it "a temporary phase of maladjustment" in 1930. Temporary can still mean years for the people living through it. About the accord What is The Working Accord? A free, public set of ten rules for bringing AI into a workplace fairly: human sign-off, no secret monitoring, shared time savings, and notice, retraining and severance before any job is cut. Workers sign to say the rules are the floor; employers sign all ten as a commitment. Read the rules . Who is behind The Working Accord? It was started by mode40, a software company in Winnipeg, Manitoba, led by Cameron Bergen and Tracy Gromniski. mode40 makes software that uses AI, and says so on its About page. Every number on the site links to its original source. Who's behind it . Why would a company that makes AI software write this? Because its founder, Cameron Bergen, spent more than 20 years running operations inside one of Canada's largest primary food processors, and saw that how a change is handled decides whether people are lifted or hurt by it. The accord is voluntary and isn't a substitute for law. It's a public floor that mode40 intends to sign first, in writing, where anyone can check it, and any other employer can sign the same ten rules.

## Who's Behind The Working Accord: Started by mode40
URL: https://workingaccord.ca/about/

Home / Who's behind it Why mode40 started the accord The Working Accord was started by mode40, a software company in Winnipeg, Manitoba. Its founder, Cameron Bergen, spent more than 20 years inside one of Canada's largest food processors, where he and Tracy Gromniski built the data systems the plants ran on. They have already watched software take over part of the work. The accord is what they learned, written down. On this page Twenty years on the plant floor What we saw Why we started the accord Our stake in this Other employers How this site was made Twenty years on the plant floor mode40 didn't start as a software company. Cameron Bergen, our founder and CEO, spent more than 20 years running operations inside one of Canada's largest primary food processors. Tracy Gromniski, now our Chief Product Officer, worked alongside him there, building the data and machine-learning systems the plants ran on, years before anyone was calling it AI. So when people ask what happens to work when software starts doing part of it, we're not guessing. We were there. What we saw Some jobs went. We won't pretend otherwise. Not everyone who left landed well, and we don't think anyone should write about this subject without saying so. We also watched people rise. Shift supervisors who used to lose the first hour of every shift to spreadsheets started spending it on the floor with their crews. Maintenance stopped being the team that showed up after something broke and became the team that decided when to fix it. Schedulers started asking the system harder questions than the engineers did, because they knew where the real constraints were. The people who did best weren't the most senior or the most technical. They were the ones who got curious about the new system, asked what it was seeing, and learned to tell when it was wrong. Give someone the time and training to do that, and they go further than anyone expected, including them. The difference between a change that lifted people and one that frightened them was rarely the software. It was whether people were told early, trained properly, and given a share of what it saved. Why we started the accord Most of what's said about AI and work right now comes from people selling it or people worried about it, often with good reason. We make software that uses AI, so we're not neutral, and we say so here. But we've watched this change up close for two decades, and we've made up our minds. Cutting jobs is not a reason to use AI. A plan whose point is a smaller payroll isn't a plan. When software changes someone's job, they're owed notice, retraining and a fair share of what it saves. So we wrote that down as ten rules, and we're putting our name on them in public, where anyone can hold us to them. Our ask of any other employer is the same as our ask of ourselves: sign all ten rules, or don't sign. No picking the easy ones. mode40 intends to be the first employer to sign, and we'll post the date here when we do. Our stake in this mode40 makes software that uses AI, so we have a stake in how this goes. This site is advocacy, not research. That's why every number about jobs and wages links to its original source, and why the commitments here are ones anyone can hold us to. One mode40 example today: AI tools draft much of our writing, and a named person approves every word that goes out, including this page. Who's accountable. The accord is led by Cameron Bergen, mode40's founder and CEO, and Tracy Gromniski, mode40's Chief Product Officer. mode40 is responsible for every line on this site. Corrections and questions: marketing@mode40.com . Other employers The accord is mode40's public commitment, and it's open to any employer that wants to make the same one. There's no fee and nothing to buy. An employer signs all ten rules or doesn't sign, and is listed with the date on the signers page . If a worker reports that a signer broke a rule, we ask the employer to answer and note on the list that a question was raised and whether they answered. We publish the count of reports every quarter and never publish the worker's name. How this site was made Drafted, researched and fact-checked with Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, which also sells AI. So don't take our word or its word. Every number links to the original paper on the sources page , along with who paid for each study. A person at mode40 chose and approved every line. That's rules 2 and 4, applied to ourselves. ## Privacy: The Working Accord
URL: https://workingaccord.ca/privacy/

Home / Privacy Privacy If you sign, we use your name and email to confirm and count your signature, and for nothing else. We don't sell it, share it with any company, or add you to a marketing list. Workers' names are never published. What we collect: your name, email, whether you're signing as a worker or employer, your organization (employers only), and optionally your province. What we publish: employers' names and signing dates. Never workers' names. What we don't do: sell or share your details, or send you marketing. You'll get one email to confirm your signature. Removing your name: email marketing@mode40.com and we'll delete your signature and details. No tracking: this site uses no advertising cookies or trackers. This concept version of the site stores nothing: the form checks what you type and then discards it.
